title: Statistics for Physical Sciences and Engineering
description: The Statistics Department's service course for science and engineering students (taught with STA 201 and STA 204): variables, data and sampling, descriptive statistics, counting methods, probability, random variables and distributions, mathematical expectation, and statistical inference. Built from Dr S. O. Oyamakin's STA 201/202/204 lectures 1 to 6 and the probability distributions guide in the course folder.

topics.title: Variables, Data and Sampling
topics.summary: Statistics studies variables measured on samples to learn about populations. Variables are discrete or continuous, categorical (nominal or ordinal) or scale, and continuous measurements have real limits. A statistic describes a sample and a parameter a population, and samples are drawn by random or non-random methods.
subtopics: Discrete and continuous variables; real limits

topics.title: Descriptive Statistics
topics.summary: Descriptive statistics summarise data with measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), measures of position (quartiles, deciles, percentiles), measures of dispersion (range, quartile deviation, variance, standard deviation) and graphs such as bar charts, histograms and stem-and-leaf displays. Skewness compares the mean and median.
subtopics: Range, quartile deviation, variance and standard deviation
Graphs: bar charts, histograms and stem-and-leaf

topics.title: Counting: Permutations and Combinations
topics.summary: Counting the possible outcomes uses the multiplication rule: an operation of two steps done in n1 and n2 ways can be done in n1·n2 ways. Permutations count ordered arrangements, combinations count unordered selections, and identities such as C(n, r) = C(n, n − r) relate them.
subtopics: Permutations with repetition and of like objects

topics.title: Probability, Conditional Probability and Bayes' Theorem
topics.summary: Random phenomena are unpredictable in each trial but show long-run regularity. Probability is defined on a sample space of outcomes, with addition rules for unions, the multiplication rule and independence, conditional probability P(B|A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A), the total probability rule and Bayes' theorem.

topics.title: Random Variables and Probability Distributions
topics.summary: A random variable takes values with probabilities given by a probability mass function (discrete) or density function (continuous), with a cumulative distribution function F(x). Key distributions are the binomial, Poisson, uniform and normal; the normal is standardised by z = (x − μ)/σ.

topics.title: Mathematical Expectation
topics.summary: The expected value E(X) is the probability-weighted mean of a random variable. Expectation is linear, so E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b. The variance is E(X²) − [E(X)]², with Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X), and moments about the origin and the mean describe a distribution's shape.
subtopics: The mean (expected value) of a random variable
Expectation of a function of X
Moments about the origin and the mean

topics.title: Sampling Distributions, Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
topics.summary: Inference uses samples to draw conclusions about populations. The standard error of the mean is σ/√n. Estimators are unbiased when their expected value equals the parameter, and confidence intervals give ranges likely to contain it. Hypothesis tests weigh evidence against a null hypothesis, risking Type I and Type II errors, using z, t, chi-square tests, correlation and regression.
subtopics: Type I and Type II errors
